one_liner: Zig thread-per-core io_uring server for the core NATS pub/sub protocol; ~1.4x Go nats-server publish rate in its own benchmark.
what_it_does: BusterMQ is a standalone broker that speaks the core NATS text protocol (CONNECT, PUB, SUB, UNSUB, PING/PONG) on port 4222, so an unmodified NATS client can use it for plain fire-and-forget pub/sub; you run it in place of nats-server, and there is no library API. It adds an opt-in '+ROUTE' extension: a client that sends shard_aware:true in CONNECT is told which per-worker port (4223 and up) owns each subject and can move that subscription there. JetStream, queue groups, message headers (HPUB), TLS, auth and clustering are not implemented.
how_it_is_fast: Thread-per-core: one worker per core, pinned with sched_setaffinity, each with its own io_uring ring (optional SQPOLL or --busy-poll spinning), its own SO_REUSEPORT listener, and its own clients and subscriptions. Reads land in 64 KB reference-counted mbufs from a prefaulted pool, and publishes needed on other cores are forwarded as offset descriptors over an N x N matrix of lock-free SPSC queues with eventfd wakeups, so the payload is not copied between cores. Sends are batched once per loop iteration per client, payloads of 4 KB or more go out as scatter-gather IORING_OP_SENDMSG_ZC straight from the shared mbuf, and subject lookup uses a 64-bit rapidhash key in a per-worker routing cache fronted by a 256-bit Bloom filter. The +ROUTE extension removes the cross-worker hop by steering each subscriber to the worker that owns its subject (subject hash mod worker count).
when_to_use: Studying or prototyping thread-per-core io_uring broker design: the Zig source is compact and ships with a deterministic-simulation (VOPR-style) test harness.
Ephemeral core-NATS fan-out of small messages (the benchmark used 128 B) on one Linux box with dedicated cores, where at-most-once delivery with silent drops is acceptable.

Latency-sensitive fan-out on dedicated cores that can spin at 100% CPU: in the saturated benchmark, --busy-poll cut p99 from 92.55 ms to 21.22 ms and raised the publish rate from 2.98M to 4.72M msg/s over the standard mode.
Clients you control and can teach +ROUTE, with subjects that map cleanly to single workers; this was the fastest mode in the README (6.78M msg/s).
when_not_to_use: Production messaging. The project is a single 'first commit' tagged 0.1.0-alpha, and the author said on HN it is 'not a nats replacement' and that he has no time to maintain it. The original bustermq/bustermq repo and bustermq.sh are gone, and the catalogued URL is a third-party copy.
Anything that needs JetStream or persistence, queue groups, headers, TLS, auth, clustering or leaf nodes, or payloads over 64 KB (max_payload is 65536).

Workloads with heavy subscription churn, such as request/reply inboxes with unique subjects. The first SUB to a new subject on a worker, every wildcard SUB and each last UNSUB bump a global version under a mutex, and then every worker rebuilds its whole routing cache. UNSUB also linearly scans all of that worker's subscriptions.

Memory-constrained or container deployments. By default it prefaults a 2 GB mbuf pool, reserves an N x N matrix of 131,072-entry SPSC queues (about 1 GiB at 16 workers; derived from 256 queues x 131,072 x 32-byte descriptors) and reserves a 16 MB send buffer per connection.

Hosts with more than 64 hardware threads (worker bitmasks are u64), and kernels older than 6.1 if you publish payloads of 4 KB or more: that path uses IORING_OP_SENDMSG_ZC, which liburing documents as available since 6.1, while the README only asks for Linux 5.10+.

integration.form: source-drop (standalone server binary built with Bazel; no library API)
integration.dependencies: Bazel with rules_zig 0.12.2 (hermetic Zig toolchain), rules_cc, bazel_skylib, aspect_bazel_lib, rules_oci, rules_distroless; libc (-lc); freref/spsc-queue fetched at a pinned git commit; vendored rapidhash.h
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.15.2 (pinned in MODULE.bazel); .bazelversion pins Bazel 7.6.0 although the README says Bazel 8+
integration.platforms: Linux only (io_uring; README says 5.10+, but payloads of 4 KB or more need SENDMSG_ZC, available since 6.1). Bazel platforms are declared for x86-64 and aarch64, but it was benchmarked only on x86-64 (Ryzen 9 9950X). Listeners are IPv4 only.
integration.thread_safety: Not a library. Internally each worker owns its clients and subscriptions, cross-worker traffic goes through SPSC queues, the global routing index sits behind a mutex, and the mbuf pool is a shared lock-free free list.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — standard NATS clients can connect and use core PUB/SUB/UNSUB on 4222, but queue groups, headers, TLS/auth, clustering, JetStream and payloads over 64 KB are missing, and it also binds one extra port per worker (4223 and up).

gotchas: Queue-group SUBs are parsed but the group is ignored, so every member gets every message instead of one of them. HPUB is rejected as an invalid command.

Messages are dropped silently, with only a stats counter bumped, when a client's 16 MB send buffer, a cross-worker SPSC queue, or the 1,024-forwards-per-read-batch limit is full. There is no slow-consumer disconnect. The optional --overflow queue (1,024 messages) gives up per-client ordering.

Exact subscriptions are keyed only by the 64-bit rapidhash of the subject, with identity equality and no string compare at delivery, so a hash collision would deliver to the wrong subscribers. The default starts one worker per detected CPU even though bitmasks cap it at 64 workers.
-h/--host is accepted but ignored (listeners always bind 0.0.0.0). All heap allocations, including the per-SUB subject and SID copies, go through std.heap.page_allocator.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only if you specifically need the NATS core wire protocol: it is the only catalogued entry that speaks NATS, but it is an unmaintained prototype. For a thread-per-core io_uring message system with persistence and an active project, Apache Iggy is the sibling to use; to build your own thread-per-core io_uring server, start from monoio or ringline instead.
verified_claims_summary: In a single first-party run on one AMD Ryzen 9 9950X over localhost (16 server threads and 16 client threads; 10 publishers, 10 subscribers, 10 subjects, 50M 128-byte messages sent open-loop, so the latencies are queueing delay at saturation), BusterMQ on the standard protocol published 2.98M msg/s at 4.03 GB/s with p50 11.43 ms, against Go nats-server's 2.16M msg/s, 2.94 GB/s and p50 55.70 ms (about 1.38x). The bench client spread BusterMQ connections across its per-worker ports (-w 16) while nats-server took all of them on 4222, the 6.78M msg/s (~3.1x) headline needs +ROUTE and its own client, and BusterMQ was built with Zig 0.15.2 ReleaseFast per the repo config while nats-server's version and config and the kernel are not stated.
status_note: One commit (2026-01-01), still 'active' only by the 12-month rule: the author disclaimed maintenance, the original repo and site are gone, and this URL is a third-party copy. It is Apache-2.0 and small enough to read or vendor as reference code, not as a maintained server.
